# Benchmark Results Specification

This document states what the project publishes from its CI benchmarks, how each published figure is defined, and why. [references/benchmark_site.md](../references/benchmark_site.md) describes the workflow, the file formats, and local preview.

## Where Results Appear

- **README.** The benchmark section is a summary only: a chart of mean time against run-to-run variation, the fastest algorithm for each category and input pattern, and a link to the workflow run. A full Benchmark workflow run regenerates it. The full BenchmarkDotNet tables are not in the README: the site and the `benchmark-data` branch hold every case, and the tables of the other classes had grown to about 475 KB, close to the size GitHub renders, while the Scaling class alone has about 2,100 rows. The tables of a run remain in its workflow artifacts until they expire.
- **Benchmark site.** A static site on GitHub Pages reads the published run files. It has seven views: Leagues, Explorer, Compare, Complexity, Patterns, Stability, and History. It opens on Leagues, because a first visit asks which sort is fastest; Explorer's single class, size, and pattern answer a narrower question. On a phone, each view shows its ranking, matrix, or chart in the first screen; explanations are one sentence, with the rest behind a disclosure.
- **SortVivo** ranks algorithms in the browser through WebAssembly. Those numbers depend on the viewer's machine. The CI results are the machine-fixed counterpart.

## Measurement Environment

The workflow runs on a GitHub-hosted runner and fails early unless the CPU model is the pinned one and the runner has AVX-512. Absolute times are valid only for that model and instruction set. The site therefore compares a run only with earlier runs on the same machine, which is the CPU model together with the JIT's x86-64 level (x86-64-v4 has AVX-512). The reported clock still differs between runners of one machine, so History can also divide each run's time by the `DotnetSort` of the same run, class, size, and pattern; the clock then cancels out. All benchmark classes run one after another in the same job.

## Published Figures

| Figure | Definition | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Mean | BenchmarkDotNet mean time for one sort | The primary speed measure |
| Error | Half-width of the 99.9% confidence interval | Shown as error bars. When two intervals overlap, the two results are not distinguished. |
| CV | StdDev / Mean within one run | The stability measure. CV below 2% is stable, below 5% is noisy, and 5% or more is unstable. |
| Allocated | Managed bytes per sort from `MemoryDiagnoser` | Pooled buffers do not appear after warmup. A nonzero value therefore signals a broken allocation guarantee, not the size of an auxiliary buffer. |
| Per-iteration measurements | Every measured iteration, outliers included | Shows bimodal or outlier-driven results that Mean ± StdDev hides |

Error and StdDev are not shown as two independent measures. Error is t·StdDev/√N, and the iteration count fixes N, so Error adds nothing to StdDev as a stability measure.

## Comparing Across Benchmark Classes

- The Ratio column of each class uses that class's own baseline. Never compare Ratio across classes. `ScalingBenchmark` has no baseline and so no Ratio column.
- Every class measures `DotnetSort` (`MemoryExtensions.Sort`) as a shared reference. The reference is never ranked. The site can scale each class's times by one factor so that its reference matches the reference in Partition. The factor is the geometric mean of the reference ratios over every size and pattern that both classes measured. This corrects drift between classes that ran at different times in the job. A factor for each size and pattern would instead carry the noise of a single reference measurement into every algorithm of the class.
- Overall rankings use **size leagues**. A league contains only the algorithms measured at that size. Small sizes do not separate linear sorts from O(n log n) sorts, so a single ranking at a size every class supports would mislead.
- Sizes are set per class, not per algorithm. Exchange and Selection, which are mostly quadratic, stop at 1024 and appear only in the smaller leagues. Tree and Insertion measure up to 8192 so that their non-quadratic algorithms enter the largest league. Their quadratic algorithms therefore run at 8192 too.
- Large sizes have a class of their own. `ScalingBenchmark` measures every algorithm that is not quadratic on any pattern again, at 16384, 65536, 262144, and 1048576 int elements (64 KB to 4 MB), where the input no longer fits in the inner caches. Per-method sizes would need a class per family, so a separate class keeps the other classes unchanged. Its sizes start above every other class, so no league ranks an algorithm twice, and each of its sizes is a league of its own. It shares no size with the other classes, so its times cannot be drift-corrected; Compare joins its points to each algorithm's line as measured.
- Ratios on the site divide by `DotnetSort`, not by the fastest algorithm. The fastest algorithm differs by pattern and by size, so a reader would have to look it up before a ratio means anything. Every .NET reader knows `Span.Sort`, so ×0.5 reads directly as half the time of the standard sort. `DotnetSort` is not ranked. In a league it stays at the top of the list together with the scale while the list scrolls, so that any row can be compared with it; a line marks where it would rank.
- League score: for each pattern, divide the algorithm's time by the time of `DotnetSort` in Partition, then take the geometric mean of the six ratios. All algorithms in a league share each pattern's divisor, so the order is the same as with any other common divisor; only the numbers change. The worst single pattern is shown next to the score, because a good average can hide an adversarial pattern. Where a run has no reference at that size, which happens only in some imported runs, the fastest algorithm for each pattern is the divisor, and the page says so.
- A league can be limited to comparison sorts. The Distribution class (radix, counting, bucket, and related sorts) reads the key's value and needs integer or numeric keys, and at n = 8192 three of its integer-only sorts lead the league. A reader choosing a general-purpose sort for any comparer wants the ranking without them. The scores do not change, because the divisor is the reference, not the fastest algorithm.

## Compare View

The Compare view places up to eight chosen algorithms in one chart per input pattern, with n on the x axis. This is the form that papers and sort announcements use to show where an algorithm stands. The default y value is time ÷ n log₂ n: an n log n sort stays flat, a linear sort falls, and a quadratic sort rises, so the class and the constant factor read together. Time per element and the ratio to `DotnetSort` are the alternatives. Each chart has its own y axis by default, as in papers; one axis for all six charts is an option for comparing patterns. Times from other benchmark classes carry the same per-class drift factor as Leagues. Eight series colors include pairs that are hard to tell apart where lines cross, so pointing at a line or its chip brings that algorithm forward in every chart, and a click or tap keeps it there. Any chart can be enlarged to the screen. A table below the charts lists the plotted values of one pattern, for exact numbers and for readers who cannot use the charts.

Every class measures 256 to 8192 int elements, and the Scaling class continues the lines of the algorithms that are not quadratic up to 1048576 elements (4 MB). Non-goal for now: the sizes beyond that, where papers show the input leaving the last-level cache. Each 4-fold step there multiplies the job time, so it would need a schedule of its own.

## Complexity View

The site fits k, the slope of log(time) against log(n), for every algorithm and pattern. It classifies k against reference slopes that are fitted over the same sizes. Only n (1.00) and n² (2.00) are independent of the size range; n log n is 1.14 over 256–8192 and 1.16 over 256–1024. Next to k, the view shows the Best, Average, and Worst cases from the algorithm's XML documentation. A pattern that reaches the documented worst case is therefore visible, as the textbook-fidelity rule in [AGENTS.md](../../../AGENTS.md) expects. Cells that reach ≈ n² fall into two lists. One list holds cells whose documented worst case is below n²; these need a check of the implementation. The other list holds cells within a documented worst case of n², or within a bound in another variable, such as Θ(n·m) with m distinct keys.

k also includes fixed costs, cache effects, and branch prediction. For this reason the view shows the slope of each size interval too, not only the fit over all sizes.

The detail chart draws the n, n log n, and n² guides from the selected pattern's smallest size. A pattern that follows a guide lies under it, so the guides are dashed and drawn above the data, and the labels at the right edge are moved apart. Pointing at a line brings that pattern forward; selecting it re-anchors the guides. The chart can be enlarged to the screen.

## Patterns View

The Patterns view splits what the Leagues score combines: speed on Random, and how the other patterns change that time. A quadrant chart places each algorithm on two axes:

- x: time on Random ÷ `DotnetSort`'s time on Random.
- y: time on the other patterns ÷ the algorithm's own time on Random.

y does not use the reference, so the axes do not repeat each other. An adaptive sort falls below ×1 on y at any speed on Random. By default y is the geometric mean of the other five patterns. The best, the worst, or one pattern can replace it, because a mean can hide one adversarial pattern. As in Stability, a line joins the algorithms that no other algorithm beats on both axes.

A matrix below the chart shows the ratio to Random for each pattern, on a diverging color scale around ×1. Sorted, Reversed, and PipeOrgan repeat one input in every iteration, so their ratios at small sizes include what the branch predictor learned.

## Data Retention

Each full run produces one run file. Run files are kept on the orphan branch `benchmark-data`, so that `main` does not collect data commits. The first publish imports the earlier runs from the README history; only README versions up to the 2026-11-22 Scaling run carry tables to import. Imported runs have summary statistics only, with no per-iteration measurements and no median. The three CI runs of 2026-11-22 were converted before run files named the JIT's x86-64 level; it was added to them from their workflow logs.

## Non-goals

- Comparing different machines or CPU models
- Statistical tests beyond confidence-interval overlap
- Ranking the reference sort

## Lessons Learned

- In the 2026-11-20 run, `SelectionSort` and `DoubleSelectionSort` were each measured in two classes. The two measurements differed by at most 0.9%, so drift between classes was small in that run. The reference method remains as a guard for runs where drift is larger.
- In that run, high-CV cases were scattered across algorithms and sizes instead of concentrating on particular algorithms. Treat a high CV from one run as noise until the history shows the same CV again.
- At n = 8192 the 99.9% interval is typically below 1% of the mean, so error bars mostly matter at small sizes.
- In the 2026-11-22 run, a single case with a CV above 15% compressed every other point to the bottom of a linear CV axis. The charts use a square-root CV scale.
- In the 2026-11-22 20:28 run, every CV at n = 8192 on Random was below 1%, but the Stability axis always reached at least 3%. The points shared the lower part of the chart, and the frontier labels covered each other and the step line. The axis now ends just above the largest CV.
- Earlier CI runs used three CPU models (EPYC 7763, 9V74, and 9V45), and runs on one model reported clocks from 2.60 to 3.69 GHz. Runs are therefore grouped by model and x86-64 level, not by the full processor string. The JSON report names the processor without its clock, so the converter reads the clock from the Markdown report of the same class.
- The 2026-11-22 04:43 run was the first with the reference in every class. The class factors were within 1.0% of 1. Factors for single sizes and patterns ranged up to 19.5%. The largest came from one reference cell in Partition with a CV of 6.6%, and only 4 of 180 differences exceeded the combined confidence intervals. The correction therefore uses one factor per class.
- Measuring Tree and Insertion at 4096 and 8192 lengthened the benchmark job from 17 to 26 minutes.
- The first run with `ScalingBenchmark` (2026-11-22 20:28) spent 2 h 16 min in BenchmarkDotNet. Scaling measured its 2,136 cases in 53 minutes. BenchmarkDotNet then wrote nothing for 52 minutes before it printed the summary of that class. This gap after the last case grew with about the cube of a class's case count: 7 s at 264 cases, 51 s at 528, and 3,127 s at 2,136. A synthetic class of the same shape with empty methods reproduced it. At 528 cases, the gap was 39.8 s with the baseline and the rank column, 4.4 s without the baseline, and 0.2 s without both. At 2,136 cases it was 0.5 s without both. The baseline's ratio columns and the rank column were therefore the cause. `ScalingBenchmark` has neither, and the site computes its ratios from the run file. The other classes keep both, because their gaps add up to about 2.5 minutes.
- Slopes fitted at 256 to 8192 do not predict 2^20. Before `ScalingBenchmark` was added, one sort of every algorithm and pattern was timed at 2^14 to 2^20 on a development machine. `DotnetSort` on PipeOrgan had k = 1.94 at the small sizes, yet grew 4.5- to 5-fold per 4-fold size up to 2^20: the introsort depth limit hands the bad partitions to heapsort, so the growth stays n log n. `SimdQuickSort` grew about 16-fold per step on Sorted, Reversed, and ManyDuplicates, which is quadratic, and was left out. Between 2^18 and 2^20, `HeapSort`, `TreapSort`, `BinomialHeapSort`, and `PairingHeapSort` grew 7- to 15-fold on some patterns after growing about 5-fold per step below, which points to their working set leaving the inner caches.
- With the seven default algorithms of different classes in the 2026-11-22 08:54 run, one y axis for all six patterns spanned 0.038 to 106 ns per n log₂ n. On Random, the four n log n sorts (`HeapSort`, `Driftsort`, `PDQSort`, `DotnetSort`) lay between 1.7 and 3.4 ns, a thin band of that range. An axis per chart separated them, so it became the default.
- `QuickSort` was considered as the site's baseline, because its name is the most familiar. In the 2026-11-22 08:54 run at n = 8192 it took 16.9 times as long as `DotnetSort` on PipeOrgan, where its middle-element pivot degrades toward n². A baseline with a quadratic pattern would shrink every ratio on that pattern and change meaning with n. `IntroSortDotnet`, the library's port of the runtime introsort, scored ×0.999 against `DotnetSort` in the same league, but only Partition measures it, so it cannot correct drift between classes. `DotnetSort` ranked between 45th and 46th of 95 algorithms there, so ratios fall on both sides of ×1.
- In that run, `BitonicSort` on Random input had k = 1.16, near n log n, although its comparison count is exactly (n/4)·lg n·(lg n + 1) at every size, a slope of 1.27. The same sort on Sorted input and `BitonicSortBranchless` on any input had k ≈ 1.26, with a constant time per comparison. Only the data-dependent branch on Random input made the time per comparison fall as n grew. A k below the documented order is therefore not, by itself, evidence that the implementation does less work. Compare `StatisticsContext` counts first.
- In that run, the slope from 4096 to 8192 alone was about 2 on Sorted, Reversed, or PipeOrgan input in eleven cells of seven algorithms whose documented worst case is below n², among them `TernaryHeapSort`, `SmoothSort`, `TournamentSort`, and `IntroSortDotnet`. Their comparison and write counts grew as n log n over the same interval. These patterns give every iteration the same input. Random input, which differs per iteration, showed no such step. The step is therefore consistent with the branch predictor learning the repeated input at the smaller size. A large slope on these patterns alone is therefore a timing effect until the operation counts show otherwise.
- The twelfth such cell, `StdStableSort` on Reversed input, was real work. Its insertion-sort leaves alternate between 64 and 128 elements as the recursion depth changes parity, so comparisons per element alternate between about 34 and 66 at successive powers of two. The order stays n log n, but a single interval can show a slope of 0.1 or 2.0.
- `SelectionSortSimd` is Θ(n²), yet in the 2026-11-20 run its interval slopes were 1.30, 1.59, and 1.83 from 256 to 8192. Fixed costs dominate small sizes, so a single fitted k understates the order.
- The 2026-11-22 20:28 run passed the model check on an EPYC 9V74 runner without AVX-512, which reported 2.86 GHz; the 08:54 run had AVX-512 at 3.59 GHz. Over the 2,640 cases both runs measured, the later run took a median 1.29 times as long. `SimdQuickSort`, which then uses 256-bit vectors, took 3.3 times as long on Random at n = 8192 and 14.7 times as long on Sorted. The README history already had both kinds of 9V74 runner in August 2026: the JIT reported x86-64-v3 on some runs and x86-64-v4 on others. The CPU check therefore also requires AVX-512, and each run file records the x86-64 level.
- The 2026-11-23 07:14 run had AVX-512 at 3.68 GHz. In every class, its median time was 0.774 to 0.778 times that of the 20:28 run without AVX-512. That is the ratio of the two clocks, 2.86 / 3.68 = 0.777. `SimdMergeSort` was the only exception: at the same clock, its 512-bit path was faster only at n = 256, and from n = 1024 it took a median of about 1.5 times as long as the 256-bit path. Its merge networks stored their vectors in stack memory and loaded them back at every stage. With the vectors held in locals, a local BenchmarkDotNet run measured it 1.6 to 5 times as fast, and its 512-bit path became faster than its 256-bit path. Two runs on one CPU model that differ only in AVX-512 can therefore show code whose speed depends on the vector width.
